verdicts.title: Delivery registration and device copy of 1531/1532 outlive the map object: use-after-free writes into the shared segment, and stale state on a re-created map
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from code. register_device_array (nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp:433-480) stores a raw `nv_gpu_device_array_map_impl *` and takes no reference. The only callers of inc_map_refcount are array_map_binding.cpp/.hpp and the dup path (bpftime_shm_internal.cpp:1293), and no unregister function exists. Two paths free the impl while the agent's delivery thread keeps running until atexit. (1) The tool closes the fd: syscall_context::handle_close -> bpftime_close -> close_fd -> clear_id_at -> map_free (refcount 1 -> 0) -> destroy_ptr (map_handler.cpp:1664-1668). (2) A new tool session runs begin_new_session -> reset_server_state -> clear_all. On every delivery, deliver_locked (326-333) does `__atomic_store_n(&st[GPU_MODEL_STATUS_PID]...)` and `__atomic_fetch_add(&st[GPU_MODEL_STATUS_DELIVERIES]...)` through m.map->status_words(), whether or not the values changed. It also writes dst[i] wherever the snapshot differs. Correction to the stated mechanism: the anonymous-instance block_header (16 B) sits in front of the object, and the 24-byte free-tree hook covers only that header and the vector's allocator pointer (mp_mngr; vector_alloc_holder derives from Allocator, and m_start comes after it). So m_start is most likely intact, and host_words()/status_words() still decode to the freed storage blocks, not to nullptr. Those blocks' own first 24 bytes are their free-tree hooks, so writes to dst[0..2], st[0] and st[2] corrupt the segment's free tree, or the first words of whatever object reuses the blocks. The 'NULL write SIGSEGV' outcome is unconfirmed and unlikely; segment corruption leading to a later crash in any allocating process is the realistic result. Case 2 logic is confirmed: the `made` cache returns at 509-511 before `shards = s` (526). A new impl at the same address therefore keeps shards == 0, get_max_thread_count() returns 0, and sum_array_offset returns NULL (max_thread_count < 32). For 1532, the old buffer is indexed with the new geometry. Whether the same address is reused depends on the allocator: plausible, not confirmable read-only.

verdicts.title: 1530 values are generic addresses into .local, and an eBPF atomic add on them is undefined per the PTX ISA
verdicts.reasoning: The documented rule is confirmed. ptx-isa.txt line 26571 says: "atom with scalar type may be used only with .global and .shared spaces and with generic addressing, where the address points to .global or .shared space" (red has the same rule at 27027). llvmbpf lowers BPF atomics to a generic atomicrmw (vm/llvm-jit/src/compiler_utils.cpp emitAtomicBinOp), and b_pass_output.ptx:271 shows `atom.add.u64 %rd134, [%rd133], 1;` on the result of `_bpf_helper_ext_0001`. Both 1530 paths yield a cvta.local-derived generic address: thread_local_offset in the trampoline, and the routing's direct lookup (`add.u64 %bptl_a, ..., %bpftime_tl_in`). Nothing in nv_thread_local_routing.cpp handles atom or isspacep, and no header or commit text says 1530 values must not be used with atomics. That gap matters because atomics are the normal eBPF idiom and are required on 1531/1532. The program is hypothetical so far: the prototype's own programs (pt_lat, pt_carry) use only plain loads and stores on 1530, so no run exercised it. The concrete hardware outcome (a sticky illegal-address fault) cannot be confirmed without a GPU run, and ptxas might instead reject it after inlining, which would load the module unprobed. Either way the behaviour is outside the documented semantics, which breaks the design rule.

verdicts.title: "Atomic adds only" for 1531/1532 is assumed, not checked: plain stores lose counts, and 32-bit adds make mixed-size races with the snapshot
verdicts.reasoning: Helper 1 returns plain writable pointers for 1531 and 1532 (default_trampoline.cu:288-299). The only enforcement is helper 2 returning -1 and CPU-side EPERM. Sub-claims (a) and (c) describe a program breaking a contract the code states (nv_gpu_model_maps.hpp:10-11, '64-bit atomic adds only'). That is the same class of problem as `*cnt += 1` on today's shared GPU maps, and the prototype's own pt_hist.bpf.c switches from `*c += 1` (1502) to `__sync_fetch_and_add` (1532), so the contract is known to the author. Sub-claim (b) is reachable and goes beyond that. emitAtomicBinOp emits an i32 atomicrmw for 32-bit BPF atomics (`is64 ? ... : CreateTrunc(..., getInt32Ty())`, align 4), the 1531 constructor accepts any value_size that is a multiple of 8, and the enum comment in bpftime_shm.hpp says only 'atomic adds only'. A u32-field atomic add therefore looks compliant, yet it only partially overlaps the snapshot's `ld.relaxed.gpu.u64`. PTX 8.7 requires complete overlap for operations to be morally strong, so this is a mixed-size data race, and per 8.7.2 'the axioms ... do not apply'. Summing the u64 words over shards also carries the low field into the high field. Atomic AND/OR/XOR would likewise be accepted and then summed meaninglessly. Severity is low: the contract is written down, there is no host crash, and the result is silently wrong values for programs that break or misread the contract. The 'no data race' claim holds only under that unchecked precondition.

verdicts.title: Several GPU processes on one segment overwrite each other's delivered values, and the shard count is shared across processes
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. The `made` cache is a function-local static, so each agent process (SHM_OPEN_ONLY) allocates its own device copy and registers its own delivery. Each delivery writes the same shared data_buffer through m.map->host_words() and stores its own PID (deliver_locked 316-330). With two CUDA processes under one session, the CPU therefore reads the last writer's values, A's or B's, never A+B, and nothing detects or logs this. Two corrections. First, FINAL is only ever stored as 1, so it is not 'overwritten'. It stays 1 after the first process exits while the other process keeps overwriting values, so FINAL=1 no longer means final. Second, the shard-count overflow (the shared `shards = s` at 526, then a later create_map_basic_info in A using B's larger count with A's smaller buffer) needs two GPUs whose SM counts round to different powers of two. On one GPU every process writes the same value, which is harmless. The 'one GPU process per segment' assumption appears only in a header comment (nv_gpu_model_maps.hpp:65-66) and is not enforced. Severity medium, because the multi-process loss is silent.

verdicts.title: No creation checks for 1530/1531/1532: other key sizes and 0 entries are accepted and handled as 4-byte array keys
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. check_map_attr (map_handler.cpp:1011-1061) returns 0 via `default:` for 1530-1532. The syscall server's BPF_MAP_CREATE passes attr straight to bpftime_maps_create with no pre-check, and map_init_checked constructs the new types without any checks. BPF_MAP_GET_NEXT_KEY passes the tool's attr->next_key buffer directly, and array_next_key writes `*(uint32_t *)next_key`, so a key_size of 1 or 2 overflows the tool's buffer by 2-3 bytes. Lookups read `*(const uint32_t *)key` on both CPU and GPU, so with key_size 8 keys alias modulo 2^32. A more concrete outcome for max_entries 0: array_next_key returns key 0 both for NULL and for key 0 (`0 >= 0` sets next = 0 and returns 0), never ENOENT, so a tool iterating the keys loops forever. A lookup of key 0 then returns status word 0. Severity is low because it needs a malformed map definition, and the existing GPU map types fall through the same default.

verdicts.title: Atomic adds on a thread-local (1530) value become generic atom/red on a .local address, which the PTX ISA leaves undefined
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from the code and the documents. (1) The routed direct lookup (nv_thread_local_routing.cpp:206-222) returns `selp.b64 RET, %bptl_aN, 0, %bptl_pN`, where %bptl_aN = key*value_size + %bpftime_tl_in + offset and %bpftime_tl_in is the kernel's `cvta.local.u64 %bpftime_tl, __bpftime_tl`. The trampoline path does the same (default_trampoline.cu thread_local_offset: `(char*)area + extra_buffer + idx*value_size`). Both give a generic address into the local window. (2) BPF atomic adds lower to generic `atom.add.u64 [%rdX], 1` on a helper-1 result. lat4 FMPp62 patched PTX line 2678 shows the shape, and RESULTS-draft.md:16 says so. The FMPp62 instance is on the 1531 `hist` lookup, so it shows how the lowering looks; it is not an observed atomic on a 1530 value. (3) ptx-isa.txt (atom, the description under 9.7.15.5): "atom with scalar type may be used only with .global and .shared spaces and with generic addressing, where the address points to .global or .shared space". red has the same sentence. So `__sync_fetch_and_add`/`__atomic_add_fetch` on a 1530 value is outside the documented guarantees. (4) Nothing rejects or rewrites it. `git diff --stat` touches no pass or llvmbpf file, the routing file has no atom/red/isspacep handling, and the prototype's docs (nv_gpu_model_maps.hpp, bpftime_shm.hpp comment, RESULTS-draft table, step0b README) never say 1530 values are plain-access only. The check programs avoid it only by chance: pt_lat.bpf.c and pt_carry.bpf.c use plain `*s = ...` on 1530 and `__sync_fetch_and_add` only on 1531. The repo's GPU examples use exactly this idiom on map values (threadhist-gpu-kernel-shared-map, cuda-counter, threadscheduling). This breaks the stated rule that correctness rests on documented guarantees only, and it makes the commit's claim false for such programs. Severity: the rule violation is certain and the trigger is the most common eBPF idiom. The concrete hardware outcome (illegal-address fault and a lost application context, versus silently non-atomic behaviour) is not established by any document or measurement and cannot be tested read-only. I keep high because the documented-guarantee rule is the design's central claim. The fix as proposed (isspacep.local split, or a counted refusal at load) is sound.

verdicts.title: Size of the thread-local area has no bound: one zeroing store per 8 bytes in every probed kernel; large maps stall or OOM the host in the load hook or fail application launches
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed parts. check_map_attr (map_handler.cpp ~1011-1060) returns 0 in its default case, so 1530 gets no size check, and the 1530 constructor (nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp:21-26) stores value_size/max_entries and allocates nothing. Any u32 x u32 size is accepted. create_map_basic_info sums ALL 1530 maps in the handler table (other tools' maps included) into one area. route_thread_local_maps_of_module (nv_attach_impl.cpp:973-982) passes that sum to every probed kernel that has a probe call; there is no per-kernel filter by referenced maps. nv_thread_local_routing.cpp:330-332 emits one `st.u64 [%bpftime_tl+off], 0;` line per 8 bytes, so text size and per-launch zeroing work are linear in the area. An 8 MB area means about 1M lines (~37 MB) per probed kernel, built on the hack_fatbin pool under the cuLibraryLoadData hook (load_substitution_mutex held at nv_attach_impl.cpp:139/230). The sign-extension in (c) is confirmed: MapBasicInfo::max_entries/value_size are `int` (nv_attach_impl.hpp:48-55), the handler getters return uint32_t, and line 981 does `d.max_entries = (uint64_t)m.max_entries`. A map with max_entries >= 2^31 becomes ~2^64 and the zeroing loop has ~2^61 iterations. Corrections and limits: a std::bad_alloc is caught by the pool task's `catch (const std::exception&)` (nv_attach_impl.cpp:1166) and degrades to the original image. Only the long stall and an OOM-killer kill of the host before bad_alloc (8 GB Orin, string growth by doubling) touch the host contract. Case (c) needs an absurd map size. That nvPTXCompiler rejects >512 KB of local per thread is consistent with the documented limit (cpg-compute-capabilities.txt:788-791 "Maximum amount of local memory per thread 512 KB") but was not observed. The launch failures in (d) (area x resident threads of local memory) are plausible but unverified. Medium rather than high because the harmful cases need large or absurd map sizes. Still, nothing bounds them, and a tool's map size can stall or OOM an unrelated application's load hook and cost every probed kernel local memory and zeroing even when its programs use no 1530 map.

verdicts.title: Direct-run path (bpf_main as a kernel) is not routed: helper calls keep an undefined r5, which the 1530 trampoline treats as an area address instead of returning NULL
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. run_attach_entry_on_gpu (nv_attach_impl.cpp:1272-1279) compiles bpf_main with compile_ebpf_to_ptx_from_words and filter/wrap only. route_thread_local_maps is never called there, so param4 of each helper-1/2 call is the program's r5. llvmbpf (vm/llvm-jit/src/compiler.cpp:376-385) allocates r0-r10 without zeroing them unless kernel_compatible_mode is set. An unwritten r5 is therefore LLVM undef, and in pass output it is a register stored with no prior definition (C1 b_pass_output.ptx: `st.param.b64 [param3+0], %rd16; st.param.b64 [param4+0], %rd17;` with neither defined). llvmbpf does not model helper calls clobbering r1-r5, so a program that set r5 for an earlier 5-argument helper keeps a defined non-zero value. The path is reachable: bpftimetool (tools/bpftimetool/main.cpp:245-262) runs init_attach_ctx_from_handlers, which fills nv_attach_private_data.map_basic_info = create_map_basic_info(1024) (bpf_attach_ctx.cpp:643). That table holds the 1530 entries (map_type 1530, extra_buffer = area offset), and run_attach_entry_on_gpu copies it into map_info. The trampoline then calls thread_local_offset(real_key, map_info, c), which returns NULL only for c == 0 (default_trampoline.cu: `if (area == 0 || idx >= ...) return nullptr;`). Any other c gives a wild generic pointer that the program loads or stores through. This contradicts the stated contract ("pass 0 there: their thread-local lookups return NULL"). Low severity: the outcome is indeterminate (the register may happen to be 0), the host is bpftimetool's own process and context rather than an injected application, and a 1530 map in a directly run program is an unusual combination.

verdicts.title: An atomic add on a 1530 thread-local value becomes a generic atom on local memory, which PTX does not define, and nothing rejects it
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from the code and the documents. llvmbpf lowers BPF_ATOMIC with CreateAtomicRMW at vm/llvm-jit/src/compiler_utils.cpp:376 (Monotonic, align 8). The lat4 pass output shows that it becomes a generic `atom.add.u64 [%rd55], 1` (6lQrMe:2678, on the 1531 'hist' map, fd 14, in pt_lat.bpf.c). For 1530 the direct form gives the program `selp.b64 r, %bptl_a, 0, p` with %bptl_a = %bpftime_tl_in + key*size + offset (nv_thread_local_routing.cpp:210-221). %bpftime_tl_in comes from `cvta.local.u64 %bpftime_tl, __bpftime_tl` (lines 309, 328), so r is a generic address in the local window. The helper path (thread_local_offset, default_trampoline.cu) returns the same kind of address. ptx-isa.txt:26571: 'atom with scalar type may be used only with .global and .shared spaces and with generic addressing, where the address points to .global or .shared space'; red has the same rule (27027). Nothing rejects such a program. route_function_body only rewrites callseq blocks, the trampoline does not check, and the loader does not check. The 1530 header (nv_gpu_model_maps.hpp, nv_thread_local_routing.hpp) does not forbid atomics, unlike the 1531/1532 header. Reachability caveat: the in-tree 1502 idiom (threadhist `*cnt += 1`) and pt_lat's `*s = ...` lower to plain ld/st (e.g. two st.u32 at 6lQrMe:2755-2757), which is fine on .local. The problem needs an explicit __sync_fetch_and_add or similar on a 1530 value, a plausible idiom for counters. The run-time outcome cannot be checked read-only: a fault that kills the context, a ptxas refusal that falls back to the original image, or an add that works by accident. The rating rests on the undefined use, which nothing checks and which the documented-guarantee rule forbids. Suggested fix as reported: in routed functions, use isspacep.local plus a plain ld/op/st, or refuse at load any 1530 lookup result that reaches BPF_STX|BPF_ATOMIC, with the refusal counted.

verdicts.title: The 1531/1532 'atomic adds only' contract that the no-data-race claim depends on is not enforced; plain or 32-bit accesses are mixed-size races
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. Helper 2 returns -1 for 1531/1532 (default_trampoline.cu ~366-370), but helper 1 still hands out a raw writable device pointer: sum_array_offset for 1531, array_map_offset for 1532. Nothing checks how a program uses that pointer: no load-time analysis and no routing check. The header does state the contract ('GPU programs may change with 64-bit atomic adds only (XADD)'), so for stores and 32-bit adds the gap is that the contract is not enforced, not that a claim is false. The realistic case is the in-tree 1502 idiom: example/gpu/threadhist/threadhist.bpf.c does `*cnt += 1`. Ported to 1532 ('1502's layout'), it becomes split u32 loads and stores; the pass output shows u64 map-value accesses as two ld.u32 (6lQrMe:2582-2583, 2613-2614) and two st.u32 (2755-2757). Those partially overlap the snapshot's `ld.relaxed.gpu.u64` (nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp:177). That is a mixed-size data race. ptx-isa.txt:7385 says the axioms 'do not apply if a PTX program contains one or more mixed-size data-races', and :7649 says atomicity is not guaranteed without moral strength. The CPU can therefore get a torn value. On 1531 the same `(*v)++` is a weak RMW on a shard that every warp of an SM shares (shard = (smid&mask)*32+lane), so increments are silently lost. Reads are not excluded by the stated contract ('change' only). A program read of a 1531 value (two ld.u32) racing with other threads' atom.add.u64 on the same shard is already a mixed-size race, so the 'no data race' claim in the commit message and header does not hold for allowed uses either. Only atom-vs-atom RMW atomicity survives (ptx-isa.txt:7389). The u32-fields carry issue (iii) is accurate as described. The suggested enforcement (only XADD.DW on 8-byte-aligned offsets of a tracked lookup result, otherwise refuse and count) is appropriate.

verdicts.title: The final delivery claim (g) fails when the application calls cudaDeviceReset before exit or exits with probed kernels in flight; FINAL=1 is set regardless
verdicts.reasoning: Part (i) is real. Nothing hooks cudaDeviceReset, cuDevicePrimaryCtxReset or cuCtxDestroy. The guide says cudaDeviceReset 'destroys the primary context' (cpg-intro-to-cuda-cpp.txt:721) and 'also frees all allocations' (cpg-writing-cuda-kernels.txt:276); the agent retaining the primary context does not prevent that. The guide's printf section tells users to call it before exit (cpg-legacy-12.9.txt:12544), and many CUDA samples end with it. The 1531/1532 buffers, the snapshot module and the stream are gone before the agent's atexit handler runs. Counts since the last periodic delivery are lost: up to busy/idle 20/200 ms for sum maps and 1-2 s for per-thread maps. Corrections to the report: in (i) the failed snapshot returns before line 331, so FINAL stays 0, not 1. The failure is logged and visible to a tool, but the data is still lost. The drain thread does not 'keep calling': the first failure sets s.broken (310-314) and drain_loop returns at 402, so there is at most one more launch/sync, plus a call already in flight. Calls on a destroyed context are documented to fail with CUDA_ERROR_CONTEXT_IS_DESTROYED (drv-types.txt:6405); only a call that overlaps the reset is undocumented. Part (ii), probed kernels in flight on a non-blocking stream at exit, is accurate in the code: deliver_locked syncs only s.stream and then sets FINAL=1. However, the header states 'after the application synchronized' as a precondition, and the status word is documented as 'final delivery completed'. (ii) on its own is low; (i) carries the medium rating. Fix as suggested: hook reset and destroy to stop the drain thread and deliver first, and use stream waits on noted launch events plus a distinct 'incomplete' status.

verdicts.title: (Outside this dimension) A forked child that calls exit() hangs in the atexit handler joining the parent's delivery thread
verdicts.reasoning: Partly confirmed; the stated mechanism is not. That the child hangs in s.thread.join() because 'nothing clears' the parent's thread tid is a claim about glibc internals. The finding says it was not run. As I recall, glibc's fork-child stack reclaim zeroes the tid of every other thread descriptor, which would make that join return at once. No glibc 2.39 source is on the board, so the join mechanism is recorded as unconfirmed either way. The code does confirm a hang, through a different path. nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp has no fork handler (no register_fork_handlers). The drain thread holds run_mutex for the whole of deliver_locked: launch, cuStreamSynchronize and the copy (lines 401-404). A fork that lands during a delivery leaves the child's run_mutex locked by a thread that does not exist. A child that then calls exit() runs final_delivery_at_exit, and deliver_now(true) blocks forever at line 488. wake_mutex has the same problem with a much smaller window (line 412). The hang is intermittent, about the delivery duty cycle per fork, not 'every child for good'. It also needs a child that ends with exit() rather than _exit() or exec: Python multiprocessing and posix_spawn use _exit, but C programs that call exit(127) after a failed exec do not. Without a held lock, the child still issues CUDA driver calls on the parent's context. That is undocumented, and if they succeeded the child could mark the shared status FINAL=1 with its own pid while the parent runs. Fix as suggested: record the owner pid, have a fork-child handler mark the state foreign (no join, mutexes reinitialized), and return at once from final_delivery_at_exit and deliver_now when getpid() != owner.

verdicts.title: Device scope covers only one memory synchronization domain, so the 'morally strong' claims (c) and (d) lack a run-time check
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from the documents, but it cannot occur on the target. The source is the CUDA Programming Guide, not the PTX ISA. cpg-cuda-cpp-memory-model.txt:177 relates GPU threads by device scope only 'within the same memory synchronization domain'. cpg-memory-sync-domains.txt:197-199 says cross-domain ordering needs system scope and 'this modifies the definition of thread_scope_device'. :205-207 says CC 9.0 has 4 domains, the count is 1 before 9.0, NCCL 2.16 tags launches remote, and streams can remap domains. The PTX ISA's own .gpu definition (ptx-isa.txt ~7310) has no domain caveat, so the documents disagree, and the conservative reading applies. The snapshot (`ld.relaxed.gpu.u64`, line 177) runs on s.stream in default domain 0. Probed kernels in another physical domain are then not related to it by device scope. The reads and adds are not morally strong (no single-copy atomicity), and the RMW atomicity property at ptx-isa.txt:7389 needs each scope to include the other, so cross-domain adds to one 1531 shard lose documented atomicity. prepare_locked and get_gpu_mem_buffer never query CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MEM_SYNC_DOMAIN_COUNT. This is a portability gap with no counted fallback. The Orin (CC 8.7) reports 1 domain, hence low.

verdicts.title: The zeroing memset is asynchronous on the legacy stream and nothing documented orders it before the snapshot or the probed kernels on non-blocking streams
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed against the documents, with a partial mitigation. cuMemsetD8 (nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp:531) is the synchronous-named form. drv-api-sync.txt says memset functions 'are asynchronous with respect to the host except when the target memory is pinned host memory'. The cuMemAlloc contents are not cleared, so the zeroing matters. The memset goes to the legacy stream, which does not synchronize with non-blocking streams (drv-stream-sync.txt). s.stream is CU_STREAM_NON_BLOCKING (line 249). register_device_array starts the drain thread right after, and only elapsed time (20 ms) orders the memset before the first snapshot. Partial mitigation, not noted in the report: the trampoline globals are written afterwards with a synchronous cuMemcpyHtoD from pageable memory (write_library_global, nv_attach_impl.cpp ~2399, map_basic_info is a std::vector). drv-api-sync.txt says 'a stream sync is performed before the copy is initiated' for pageable HtoD, which likely orders the memset before any probed kernel of that library can launch. The document does not name the stream, and it does not cover the snapshot stream. In practice this never fails: microseconds against 20 ms. Low. Fix as suggested: cuMemsetD8Async on the agent's stream plus cuStreamSynchronize at registration.

verdicts.title: The status lookup's acquire fence comes before the read and pairs with nothing; the tool's plain copies race with the agent's atomic stores
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. elem_lookup for status keys does `std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); return status_buffer.data() + 8 * (k - max_entries);` (lines 99-100). The caller copies the word afterwards with plain loads, so no atomic read is sequenced before the fence. Per [atomics.fences] (cxx-draft-atomics-fences.txt:37) the fence synchronizes with nothing. The FINAL store (line 332, release) is read by a plain copy, which is a C++ data race with an atomic store (intro.races, UB). Even treated as relaxed, seeing FINAL==1 does not make the next lookup's acquire load of DELIVERIES (line 107) observe the final increment, because only an acquire read of FINAL would give that edge. On aarch64 a plain LDR before an LDAR may be satisfied later, so the architecture allows the window. Data lookups return the shared pointer, and the syscall server copies words that the next delivery stores with relaxed atomics: also a C++ data race, though each aligned 8-byte word is single-copy atomic on the hardware. The window is sub-microsecond and needs a reordering across the syscall-server path, so the practical risk is negligible; low. Fix as suggested: acquire-load status words into a per-thread buffer, and copy data words with relaxed atomic loads after the acquire load of DELIVERIES.

verdicts.title: Closing a 1531/1532 map frees it while the delivery thread keeps writing through a raw pointer (use-after-free in the shared segment)
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from the code. registered_map holds a raw `nv_gpu_device_array_map_impl *map` (nv_gpu_model_maps.cpp:193) and no reference is taken. deliver_locked dereferences it on every delivery: host_words() at cpp:316, then status_words() at cpp:326, with an unconditional PID store and DELIVERIES increment at cpp:327-330. Nothing unregisters a map. The close path frees it: syscall_context.cpp:295 bpftime_close -> close_fd -> handler_manager.cpp:123 map_free. In map_handler.cpp:1553-1562, fetch_sub with prev==1 destroys the refcount, then destroy_ptr destroys the impl. The only map-ref sharers are array_map_binding and dup (bpftime_shm_internal.cpp:1292), so a GPU program holds no reference. It is even easier to reach than the reporter says. The server opens the segment with SHM_CREATE_OR_OPEN (syscall_server_utils.cpp:145) and keeps it while an agent is alive (cpp:60-110). A new tool session's begin_new_session -> reset_server_state -> clear_all (bpftime_shm_internal.cpp:1181-1191, 1601-1608) frees every old map without any explicit close, and the new session's maps are then allocated from the same allocator. The drain thread keeps writing n words plus status words, every 20 ms to 2 s, into whatever now occupies that memory. Because host_words() reads data_buffer's offset_ptr out of the freed impl itself, the write target can also be garbage, which means a wild write in the traced process. The `made` cache keyed by `this` (cpp:509-511) is also confirmed: a new map built at the same address would get the old device buffer and no new registration. This is new with the prototype. Existing GPU maps are written only by kernels, and those are switched off at the last detach (turn_off_substituted_probes); the drain thread has no such stop. The fix is right: take a shared impl reference under map_binding_mutex, or revalidate per delivery, and key `made` by something that cannot be reused. Not verified without running: the exact allocator layout after the free.

verdicts.title: cudaDeviceReset / primary-context reset is not handled: device copies and staging are freed, the final delivery fails and FINAL is never set
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. No hook exists for cudaDeviceReset, cuDevicePrimaryCtxReset or cuCtxDestroy: the grep finds only bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:423 (a release) and :596 (its own context). The documents say a reset destroys the primary context and frees all allocations (cpg-intro-to-cuda-cpp.txt:721, cpg-writing-cuda-kernels.txt:276), whatever the agent's retain does. After such a reset, s.module/s.fn, s.stream, m.device and m.staging all belong to the destroyed state. The final path is deliver_now(true) (cpp:418) -> deliver_locked -> cuLaunchKernel on s.fn. On failure it logs, sets broken and returns (cpp:310-314), and FINAL is stored only on success (cpp:331-333). So everything since the last periodic delivery is lost: 20-200 ms for sum maps, up to 1-2 s for 1532. 1532's first delivery is due one busy period (1 s) after registration (cpp:442-450), so an app shorter than that delivers nothing. Downgraded from high to medium. The loss is visible (FINAL stays 0, DELIVERIES may be 0, and an error is logged), not silent. The reporter's host-crash sub-claim (the drain thread reading pinned staging freed mid-copy) and the stale pointers in later probed loads are marked 'not verified' and cannot be confirmed read-only, so they do not carry the severity. None of the in-tree examples or prototype victims call cudaDeviceReset.

verdicts.title: The final delivery sets FINAL=1 without waiting for application GPU work, so counts can be incomplete
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed in code. The snapshot runs on the agent's own CU_STREAM_NON_BLOCKING stream (cpp:249), which per drv-stream.txt:569 has no implicit ordering with other streams. The final path launches at once (cpp:303-307) and sets FINAL=1 on success (cpp:331-333). It never waits on launch_activity events and never checks that application work completed. The header (hpp:127-128) states 'after the application synchronized' as fact, but it is an unchecked assumption about the application. So with in-flight probed kernels at exit (unsynchronized streams, or another thread still launching when main calls exit()), adds made after the snapshot are lost while FINAL=1 says the final delivery happened. Severity is low rather than medium. The loss is limited to work in flight at process termination, which the application itself did not wait for. FINAL literally means 'final delivery completed' (hpp:17-18). The amount lost is the short window between the snapshot and _exit. The suggested fix (a bounded wait on noted launches, or a distinct 'possibly incomplete' status) fits the run-time-check-with-counted-fallback rule.

verdicts.title: The final delivery calls the driver API after main, which the CUDA guide says is undefined behaviour; FINAL rests on it
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. The handler is registered with atexit (cpp:477), and the code's own comment at cpp:474-476 says its ordering against cudart's exit handler is 'Not guaranteed'. final_delivery_at_exit (cpp:408-428) calls deliver_now(true), which runs context_scope (cuCtxSetCurrent, cuThreadExchangeStreamCaptureMode), possibly prepare_locked (cuModuleLoadData, JIT on first use when the app ran under about 20 ms), then cuLaunchKernel and cuStreamSynchronize. All of this is after main. The CUDA guide states verbatim that using the CUDA interfaces 'during program initiation or termination after main' is undefined behavior, and the runtime and driver cannot detect invalid state (cpg-legacy-12.9.txt:2368, cpg-intro-to-cuda-cpp.txt:725). FINAL=1 is written only on this path, so the status that tells a tool the values are final rests on measured behaviour. That breaks the stated rule that correctness may rest only on documented guarantees, and it contradicts the commit message's claim to the same effect. The suggested fix (a guaranteed in-main delivery hooked on the app's synchronize/teardown calls, with the atexit delivery reported under a different status) is reasonable. The UB cannot be observed read-only; the verdict rests on the document text.

verdicts.title: The exit-time final delivery waits without bound, so an app exiting while a GPU-filling kernel runs can hang
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. final_delivery_at_exit joins the drain thread with no deadline (cpp:416-417), and the drain thread can be inside cuStreamSynchronize (cpp:306-307) while holding run_mutex. deliver_now then launches the final snapshot and calls cuStreamSynchronize itself, also without a deadline. Both waits need the snapshot kernel to be scheduled next to whatever the application runs. The documents say concurrent kernel execution is not guaranteed (cpg-lazy-loading.txt:247), so a kernel that occupies every SM and does not end (a persistent kernel waiting for a host flag that main will no longer set) can block exit() indefinitely. The task brief lists hanging the host as a defect, and the host-process contract asks the agent to stay a guest. Kept at medium: the impact is a permanent hang, but the precondition is uncommon, and a finite long kernel only delays exit. Not verifiable read-only: whether the same app would exit promptly without the agent, which depends on whether cudart's teardown waits for the kernel. Since the agent retains the primary context, the agent's own waits are the blocking ones either way. The fix is right: a deadline-bounded join and cuStreamQuery polling instead of cuStreamSynchronize at exit, with no FINAL and a counted skip on timeout.

verdicts.title: Fork children inherit the delivery state and the atexit handler: a child can hang at exit or call CUDA with the parent's context
verdicts.reasoning: The gap is confirmed from the code. The file has no fork handler and no owner-pid check (grep finds no register_fork_handlers or pthread_atfork in runtime/src/bpf_map/gpu). The atexit registration (cpp:477) and state() (s.ctx, s.maps, s.thread, the mutexes) are inherited. In a fork child, final_delivery_at_exit runs in this order: wake_mutex (cpp:412), then s.thread.join() on a thread that does not exist in the child (cpp:416-417), then deliver_now. deliver_now runs context_scope(s.ctx), takes run_mutex (cpp:487-488) and makes driver calls with the parent's context. No document covers CUDA use in a fork child. The reporter's scenario skips the join step. What join does on a nonexistent thread depends on glibc and on how the agent was loaded (main libc vs a dlmopen namespace) and cannot be confirmed read-only. The run_mutex hang needs the fork to land while the drain thread holds that lock. It is held for every delivery (cpp:401-404) and for the first prepare (about 240 ms, 20 ms after registration). That window is a probability qualifier, not a certainty. The pattern is also uncommon: a CUDA app forking after the first registration whose child then calls exit() rather than _exit/exec. Python multiprocessing children use os._exit. So the severity is lowered to low. The fix is correct and matches the repository's standard: an owner pid, a child marker registered via bpftime::register_fork_handlers, and an early return before any mutex, join or CUDA call.

verdicts.title: The one-GPU-process-per-segment assumption is not enforced: two agent processes overwrite each other's delivered values and FINAL
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. get_gpu_mem_buffer keeps a per-process cache (a static `made`, cpp:505-511), so every agent process allocates its own device copy and registers its own delivery (cpp:541-543). deliver_locked stores each process's shard sums into the shared host_words() whenever they differ (cpp:319-322), and stores PID and FINAL unconditionally (cpp:327-333). With two traced processes on one segment, an ordinary bpftime setup (two `bpftime start` runs, or LD_PRELOAD inherited by workers), the tool sees one process's values at a time, never their sum. The PID flips, and the first process to exit sets FINAL=1 while the other keeps overwriting. Nothing is claimed in shared memory, and nothing is logged or counted. The assumption appears only in a code comment (hpp:65-66: 'one GPU process per segment'), not in the commit message or the status. This also regresses on the IPC-based 1502 maps, where both processes' updates go through the shared CPU map. Medium is right: the results are silently wrong in normal multi-process use. The suggested CAS owner claim with counted refusal, or a per-process area, is reasonable.

verdicts.title: '64-bit atomic adds only' is not enforced: 32-bit XADD, plain read-modify-write stores and other atomics silently corrupt or undercount 1531/1532 values
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed that nothing enforces the rule. Helper 1 returns a writable pointer for 1531/1532 (default_trampoline.cu:288-299), and only helpers 2 and 3 are refused (lines 368-370, 456-458). nv_thread_local_routing.cpp and the VM have no check for these types. The LLVM JIT picks the atomic width from the opcode (vm/llvm-jit/src/compiler.cpp:1637-1647), so a 32-bit XADD becomes a 32-bit atomic that partly overlaps the snapshot's 64-bit ld.relaxed.gpu. That is a mixed-size data race, for which ptx-isa.txt:7385 says the axioms do not apply. Summing packed sub-word fields also carries between them. One correction: with struct {u32 hits; u32 inflight} on little-endian, it is ±1 on the low field (hits) that carries into inflight; the reporter's example has the fields reversed. The likeliest failure is the plain `*v += 1` idiom, which the repository's own 1502 example uses (example/gpu/threadhist/threadhist.bpf.c:27). On 1531 every warp of an SM shares the 32 lane shards, so the increments silently undercount. The prototype's own programs comply (pt_hist/pt_lat/pt_carry use __sync_fetch_and_add). Low severity, judged by the same standard as #7: hpp:11 states the restriction as a rule for program authors, not a claim that the runtime enforces it, and bpftime has no verifier. Only programs that break the stated contract go wrong, unlike #7 where ordinary use does. Still a real gap, because such a program loads and silently gives wrong counts. A load-time check, or at least documenting it in the map type, is the fix.

verdicts.title: Device-copy allocation runs on the link-instantiating thread in global capture mode with a NULL-stream memset (capture invalidation on injected or late attach)
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. create_map_basic_info is called from instantiate_bpf_link_handler_at (bpf_attach_ctx.cpp:644). That runs from init_attach_ctx_from_handlers on the agent's init thread, and from the auto-refresh thread (agent.cpp:726, 777, 1120). get_gpu_mem_buffer then calls cuMemAlloc and cuMemsetD8 (synchronous, legacy NULL stream) at cpp:530-531, and register_device_array calls cuMemAllocHost at cpp:452, all without a capture-mode exchange. The only relaxed-mode switches in the tree are the watcher (bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:285) and the drain thread's context_scope (cpp:369). In global mode, another thread's global-mode capture prohibits 'potentially unsafe' calls such as allocations (drv-stream.txt:1134-1140). A NULL-stream operation while a blocking stream captures is the documented implicit-dependency error. That this invalidates the application's capture, rather than only failing the agent's call, rests on step0b C5 claim 10 (class P, measured: 1,732-8,482 invalidations by a default-mode copier). If the allocation or memset is refused, it is logged and returns 0, so the map is disabled (helpers return NULL). The reporter's llama.cpp example is weak: ggml captures in relaxed mode on non-blocking streams. Global-mode capture is still the cudaStreamBeginCapture default (PyTorch's graphs use it). The trigger is limited to injected or late (auto-refresh) attach while the app captures, so low. Existing GPU maps already allocate on this path; the prototype adds the NULL-stream memset and the pinned staging allocation.

verdicts.title: The device copy's zeroing is not ordered before its first use: memset on the NULL stream, asynchronous, pointer published at once
verdicts.reasoning: Partly refuted. The synchronous cuMemsetD8 on device memory is asynchronous with respect to the host (drv-api-sync.txt:63), and the pointer is published at once (cpp:541-544). But probed kernels see the pointer only through map_info. Both paths write map_info with a synchronous cuMemcpyHtoD from a pageable std::vector: nv_attach_impl.cpp:1387 (late path) and the cuMemcpyHtoD helper used for 'map_info' near nv_attach_impl.cpp:2399-2417 (substitution). For pageable-to-device transfers 'a stream sync is performed before the copy is initiated' (drv-api-sync.txt). That legacy-stream sync orders the earlier legacy-stream memset, issued at link instantiation in the same context, before the copy starts, so before any probed kernel can read the new pointer. The 'probed kernel adds before the memset, then the memset zeroes them' scenario is therefore covered by a documented guarantee. One caveat: this assumes the memset and the map_info copy share a context and that link instantiation comes before the library load, as both paths do. The other half survives. The pointer also goes straight to register_device_array, and the snapshot runs on the agent's non-blocking stream (cpp:249). No API edge orders it after the memset; only the 20 ms delay and, in practice, the earlier map_info copy do. A first snapshot could therefore read uninitialised cuMemAlloc memory and deliver garbage. That is transient, since the next delivery overwrites it, unless it is the final delivery. Under the documented-only rule it still rests on timing. Low. The fix (cuMemsetD8Async on the agent's stream plus a synchronize before publishing) is right.

verdicts.title: A status-key lookup returns status words i..7 rather than 'status word i then zeros', breaking the documented status read for wide or per-thread values
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed. elem_lookup returns `status_buffer.data() + 8 * (k - max_entries)` (cpp:100), and bpf() copies get_userspace_value_size() bytes from it. That size is value_size, times gpu_thread_count for 1532 (the map_handler.cpp diff adds 1532 to that multiplication). The buffer is GPU_MODEL_STATUS_WORDS*8 + thread_count*value_size (cpp:85-86), so nothing reads out of bounds. But the bytes returned are status words i..7 followed by zeros, not 'status word i (then zeros up to a value)' as hpp:16-18 and the cpp:98 comment state. A 1531 map with value_size 16 returns {final, pid} for key max_entries+1. A 1532 map returns deliveries/final/pid as thread indices 0/1/2 of key max_entries+0. The documented contract is false whenever value_size > 8 or the map is 1532. Impact is low: the in-tree loader (proto/tools/pt_loader.c:118-127) reads only the first 8 bytes, which are correct. A tool that follows the header literally, such as one summing a 1532 value or checking the whole value, misreads it. A separate issue, not part of this finding: the status path's acquire fence comes before the caller's plain read, so it does not order a FINAL read before later value reads.
